title: The new moon
hookLine: Jewish, Muslim and Buddhist calendars follow the moon; Rabbi Joshua walks to Rabban Gamaliel on his own Yom Kippur, and the Qur'an calls new moons fixed seasons
tomorrow: a king asked the Buddha one favor about the full moon. what?

lines: SOMEONE HAD TO WATCH THE SKY.
COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.
cards: Before calendars lived in phones, someone had to watch the sky. In the days of the Mishnah's rabbis, a new month began when witnesses came to the court and said: we saw the new moon.
The Mishnah tells of one month when the rabbis disagreed about the witnesses. Rabbi Joshua thought Rabban Gamaliel had accepted bad testimony, which would move the date of Yom Kippur.
So Gamaliel sent him an order: come to me with your staff and your money on the day your own count says is Yom Kippur.

teach.h: JOSHUA WALKS IN ON HIS OWN YOM KIPPUR.
teach.b: Carrying a staff and money would break the holy day as Joshua counted it. He was distressed. Rabbi Akiva pointed him to a verse: "which ye shall proclaim in their seasons."
The rabbis read it this way: the holy days are the ones the court proclaims. So Joshua took his staff and his money and walked to Gamaliel on his own Yom Kippur.
Gamaliel stood, kissed him on the head, and said: come in peace, my teacher and my disciple. That is the teaching the rabbis drew: in Judaism, holy time isn't only read off the sky.
It's set by a community that watches the moon together and agrees to keep the same days.

teach.h: ROSH CHODESH: THE HEAD OF THE MONTH.
teach.b: Today the Jewish calendar is calculated in advance, but the new month is still marked as Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month, with its own prayers. Many Muslims still watch for the same thin crescent.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "They ask thee, (O Muhammad), of new moons, say: They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage."
The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his followers to begin and end the fast of Ramadan by sighting the new moon. That's the shared thing: a month that begins by looking up, together.
And the honest difference: the Jewish calendar adds a month in some years to keep its festivals in their seasons, so Passover stays in spring.
The Islamic calendar follows the moon alone, so Ramadan travels slowly through the seasons.

how: Jews mark Rosh Chodesh, the new month, with added prayers in the synagogue; Muslims look for the new crescent to begin and end Ramadan, and communities announce the sighting. Buddhist observance days also follow the moon.

s: the Jewish month and the Islamic month both begin with the new moon
the court declared the month on witnesses' word; Ramadan begins when the crescent is sighted.
he came with his staff and money on his own Yom Kippur, and Gamaliel kissed his head.
Ramadan falls in the same season every year
the Islamic calendar follows the moon alone, so Ramadan moves through the seasons.

games.q: your neighbor's Ramadan starts a day later than her cousin's in another city. what fits today's teaching?
o: both are waiting for the crescent; communities can sight it on different days.
one of them must be using the wrong calendar app.
it's a mistake: Ramadan begins on the same date everywhere.
games.why: the month begins by sighting the new moon, and communities may see it, or accept the sighting, on different evenings.

practice: Find out when the next new moon falls and put a small mark on that day. On the first evening or two after it, you could look west just after sunset for the thinnest crescent.
For now, rest your eyes on the nearest window or wall, and picture that dark sky waiting to be watched.

wordCard.voice: The new moon: the start of the month in the Jewish and Islamic calendars, once declared on witnesses' word, and still watched for by many.

orig.note: Hebrew: head of the month, the new-moon day in the Jewish calendar.

carryVoice: Something to carry: the new moon, a month that starts when people look up together. See you next time.

Calendar practice: the Jewish calendar adds a leap month (Adar II) in some years so Passover stays in spring (cf. Deuteronomy 16:1, the month Abib); the Islamic calendar is purely lunar, so Ramadan moves through the seasons
